articles.text: LǏ PÍNG: Nǎinai, nín zhēn zǎo. Wǒ mā ne?
LǏ PÍNG: You're up so early, Grandma. Where's Mom?
NǍINAI: Tā ya, chūqu mǎi cài le. Érzi huílai le, zǒng yào duō mǎi diǎnr cài ma! Nǐde péngyou ne? Tā hái méiyou qǐlai ba?
GRANDMOTHER: Oh, she went out to buy some groceries. When a son comes back, you've always got to buy some extra food. Where's your friend? He's not up yet, is he?
LǏ PÍNG: Qǐlai le, xǐ liǎn ne.
LǏ PÍNG: Yes, he's up. He's washing his face.
NǍINAI: Xiǎo Píng a, nǐde péngyou jiào shénme míngzi? Wǒ yòu wàng le.
GRANDMOTHER: Xiǎo Píng, what's your friend's name? I've forgotten it again.
LǏ PÍNG: Jiào "Tāngmǔ."
LǏ PÍNG: "Tom."
NǍINAI: Ng, "Tāngmǔ," hái hǎo jì. Nǐ hé tā shuō, dàole zánmen jiā, jiù shi yìjiā rén, shénme shìr dōu bié kèqi. Tā yí kèqi, wǒ jiù bù zhīdào zěnme bàn hǎo le.

GRANDMOTHER: Hm, "Tom," that's fairly easy to remember. You tell him that in our house he's just part of the family and he shouldn't be polite about anything. Once he starts in with the politeness, I won't know what to do.
LǏ PÍNG: Wǒmen huílai yǐqián zài Tāngmǔ jiā zhùle liǎngtian, tā bàba māma duì wǒ hěn hǎo. Tāngmǔ rén yě hěn hǎo, zài Měiguode shíhou, tā gěi wǒ bù shǎo bāngzhu.
LǏ PÍNG: Before we came back we stayed at Tom's house for a couple of days. His parents were very nice to me. Tom is also a very good person; when we were in America, he helped me a lot.

NǍINAI: Ou, zhèiyàng hǎo, niánqīng rén yīnggāi hùxiāng bāng máng. Āi! Jìde nǐ yéye zài Rìběn nèi shíhou, pīnmìng niàn shū, rénjia Rìběn rén háishi kànbuqǐ ya, nǎr yǒu shénme Rìběn péngyou. Zhǐ hǎo jǐge Zhōngguo xuésheng zhù zài yìqǐ. Āi!

GRANDMOTHER: Mm. That's good. Young people ought to help each other out. (Sigh) I remember when your grandfather was in Japan, he studied like crazy, but those Japanese still looked down on him. He didn't have any Japanese friends to speak of. The Chinese students just had to live together. (Sigh)
LǏ PÍNG: Nǎinai, guòqùde shì jiù bié qù xiǎng ta le.
LǏ PÍNG: Grandma, don't go thinking about things from bygone days anymore.
NǍINAI: Xiànzài hǎodeduō le, nǐ zài wàibianr niàn shū, wǒ bú nàme dānxīn le...
GRANDMOTHER: These days, it's much better. I don't worry so much about you out there studying...
TĀNGMǓ: Lǐ Nǎinai, nín zǎo!
TOM: Good morning, Grandma Lǐ!
NǍINAI: Zǎo, Tāngmǔ. Zuòle yìtiān fēijī bù duō shuì yìhuǐr?
GRANDMOTHER: Good morning, Tom. After a day on the airplane don't you want to get some more sleep?
TĀNGMǓ: Shuìgòu le. Lǐ Nǎinai, nín zuòzhe ba, wǒmen bāng nín shōushi.
TOM: No, I've gotten enough sleep. Grandma Lǐ, you sit down, we'll straighten up for you.
NǍINAI: Duō yǒu lǐmàode háizi!
GRANDMOTHER: What a well-mannered child!
TĀNGMǓ: Lǐ Nǎinai, nín hé érzi, érxífur zhù zài yìqǐ, sūnzi, sūnnǚ yě cháng lái, nínde fúqi zhēn hǎo.
TOM: Grandma Lǐ, you're so fortunate to live with your son and daughter-in-law, and to have your grandson and granddaughter come often.
NǍINAI: Shéi shuō bú shì ne? Wǒ cháng shuō, wǒmen jiāde fúqi dōu shi wǒ nà xiàoshùnde érxífur dàiláide.
GRANDMOTHER: That's for sure. I often say that the good fortune of our family was all brought to us by that filial daughter-in-law of mine.
LǏ PÍNG: Wǒ nǎinai yòu gāi shuō wǒmen jiāde lìshǐ le.
LǏ PÍNG: Here goes Grandma telling our family history again.
TĀNGMǓ: Lǐ Nǎinai, zhèixiē shìr nín gěi wǒ jiǎngjiang xíng bu xíng?
TOM: Grandma Lǐ, could you tell me about these things?

NǍINAI: Hǎo wa. Shuōqilai huà jiù cháng le. Wǒ hé Xiǎo Píng yéye dōu shi Shěnyáng rén. Rìběn rén láile yǐhòu, cáichǎn ya, tǔdì ya, dōu bù néng guǎn le, líkāi jiā pǎo dàole Nánfāng. Xiǎo Píng bàba zài Shànghǎi niàn shū cái rènshile wǒmen zhèige érxífu.

GRANDMOTHER: Sure! It's a long story. Xiǎo Píng's grandfather and I are both from Shěnyáng (Mukden). When the Japanese came, we couldn't bother with our property or land any more; we left our home and fled to the South. Xiǎo Píng's father didn't meet our daughter-in-law until he was going to school in Shànghǎi.
TĀNGMǓ: Nèi shíhou nǚháizi shàng dàxuéde duō bu duō?
TOM: Were there many women who went to college in those days?
NǍINAI: Méiyou xiànzài zhème duō. Wǒmen érxífu jiā xiāngdāng yǒu qián, érqiě yídàjiā rén yǒu qībāshíge, zài Sūzhōu shéi dōu zhīdao tāmen jiā.
GRANDMOTHER: Not as many as there are now. My daughter-in-law's family was quite rich, and there were seventy or eighty people in that one big family. Everyone in Sūzhōu knew them.
TĀNGMǓ: Zhèiyàngrde jiātíng guīju yídìng bù shǎo.
TOM: A family like that must have had a strict code of behavior.

NǍINAI: Shéi shuō bú shì ne! Tāmen jiāde xiǎojie bù néng zài wàibianr niàn shū, zhǐ néng qǐng lǎoshī dào jiāli jiāo diǎnr Sì Shū shénmede. Xiǎo Píng mǔqin juéde yíge fùnǚ yào zài shèhuìshang dúlì, yídìng děi chūqu niàn shū. Jiù zhèiyàng, tā cái pǎo dào Shànghǎi niàn shū qu le.

GRANDMOTHER: You bet they did! Their young ladies couldn't go to school outside the home: they could only hire a teacher to come to the house and teach them a little of the Four Books and so forth. Xiǎo Píng's mother felt that if a woman wanted to be independent in society, she had to leave home to study. That's why she ran away to Shànghǎi to go to school.
TĀNGMǓ: Zài nèi shíhou, zhēn bù róngyi.
TOM: That must have been really hard back then.

NǍINAI: Zài dàxuéde shíhou, Xiǎo Píngde fùmǔ shi hěn hǎode péngyou, kěshi zěnme bàn ne? Wǒmen shénme dōu méiyou le, yě méiyou qián. Zìjǐde érzi zěnme néng hé zhèiyàngr yíwèi xiǎojie jiéhūn ne? Xiǎo Píng mā bú nàme xiǎng...

GRANDMOTHER: When they were in college, Xiǎo Píng's parents were very good friends, but what were we to do? We didn't have a thing left, and we didn't have any money. How could our own son marry a young lady like that? But Xiǎo Píng's mother didn't think so...
TĀNGMǓ: Tā zěnme xiǎng?
TOM: What did she think?
NǍINAI: Tā shuō tā yào zhǎo yíge zìjǐ xǐhuande rén jiéhūn, dìwèi hé qián dōu bú zhòngyào. Āi, tā chīle duōshao kǔ cái líkāile nèige dà jiātíng.
GRANDMOTHER: She said she wanted to find a person she herself liked to get married to, and that status and money weren't important. (Sigh) What she went through to leave that big family.
TĀNGMǓ: Nà, nǐmen zěnme dào Xiānggǎng lái le ne?
TOM: Well then, how did you come to Hong Kong?

NǍINAI: Tāmen zài Yīngguó niànwán shū jiù lái Xiānggǎng zuò shì, yìnián yǐhòu yòu bǎ wǒmen jiēlai le, zhèiyàngr yìjiā rén cái zài Xiānggǎng zhùxialai le. Xiànzài wǒ niánji dà le, jiāli dà shìr xiǎo shìr dōu shi Xiǎo Píng mǔqin guǎn. Nǐ shuō wǒ fúqi hǎo, zhēn shi yìdiǎnr yě bú cuò.

GRANDMOTHER: When they finished school in England they came to Hong Kong to work; a year later they brought us out, and then our whole family settled here. Now that I'm getting on in years, Xiǎo Píng's mother takes care of all the big and small matters here at home. So when you say I'm blessed with good fortune, you're absolutely right.
LǏ PÍNG: Nǎinai, wǒ mā kuài huílai le ba?
LǏ PÍNG: Grandma, Mom will be home soon, won't she?
NǍINAI: Kuài huílai le, wǒmen qù bǎ zǎofàn nònghǎo ba.
GRANDMOTHER: Yes. Let's go get breakfast ready.
TĀNGMǓ HÉ LǏ PÍNG: Hǎo, zǒu ba.
TOM AND LǏ PÍNG: Okay, let's go.
